method: Single printed items split from the automatic families of 1782, and of 1781 where they reach the 1782 pages (long-running ones included), every item in 3 or more papers counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page, papers that comparison missed looked for again and read, a sweep of word-for-word passages shared by 4 or more papers for items the families miss, phrase searches on all 1,509 pages of 1782 in both transcriptions for every admitted and chosen item, and scan checks of each admitted passage, by the thin-year rule (Y-THIN as amended on 23 November 2026: an item printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4, is eligible; items printed by every surviving paper are admitted, the others chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news)
scan_scope: Each crop covers the excerpt, the opening of the printed item. Long documents were not proofread in full.

new_groups.label: Congress, 4 October 1782: 'Resolved unanimously, That congress are sincerely desirous of an honourable and permanent peace' and will conclude neither a separate peace nor a truce

new_groups.label: General Greene's letters of 28 and 29 August 1782, with General Leslie's letter on provisions and General Gist's report of the skirmish of 27 August

It is very unfortunate that we have to lament the loss of so valuable and distinguished an officer as lieutenant colonel Laurens, who was killed in the skirmish on the 27th instant'), with General Gist's report and a list of the killed and wounded. dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1782 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 550 items printed somewhere). The same script was run with year 1781 over the 1782 pages (items_from_1781.json: 47 items, 5 of them in 4 or more papers by the finder's count). Every finder item in 3 or more papers was counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page of 1782 in both transcriptions (a page prints the item when it holds at least 18 of the opening's word 5-grams), and texts read from different printings were merged (395 texts). For every text at the bar or one paper short of it, the papers the comparison missed were looked for again on their pages (the best page within the text's weeks) and read. A sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers, over every page, found items the families miss (as X-1803-09); each was read. Every admitted and chosen item was then counted by phrase searches of its opening over all 1,509 pages in both transcriptions, and every hit read (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json).
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35, a target, not a quota); digests are not admitted. In 1782, 22 items are printed by every paper that survives for their weeks, 19 of them from September to December, when only the four year-round papers survive; 13 items are chosen, in 11 stories, so that every month from January to September has one.
dispositions_summary.paper_counting: 1782 has 8 catalogue series, which are 8 papers: no paper is under two catalogue numbers. The Pennsylvania Packet (Philadelphia, three a week, 157 issues), the Connecticut Courant (Hartford; Tuesdays, 53), the New-Jersey Gazette (Trenton; Wednesdays, 52) and the New-Hampshire Gazette and General Advertiser (Portsmouth; Saturdays, 52) run all year; the Royal Gazette (Charleston, held by the British) to 3 August (62 issues); the New-Jersey Journal (Chatham) survives in 9 issues, the Royal South-Carolina Gazette (Charleston) in 3 and the New-York Gazette, and the Weekly Mercury (New York, held by the British) in 2. Papers in print in any three weeks: 4 to 7; 7 in March, 5 or 6 in most windows from January to July, and only the four year-round papers in 67 windows, most of them from August on.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: By the first 40 words of their openings, the eligible items not chosen are as listed in not_admitted (with their counts). The admitted and chosen items were counted by phrase searches of their openings and every hit read; their counts and the papers that survive for their weeks are in the README's table of stories.
counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains items printed together: the King's speech of 27 November 1781 with the addresses of both Houses, the King's answer to the Lords and Lord Cornwallis's letter; General Greene's letters of 21 and 31 May; Congress's resolutions of 4 October with General Greene's letters of August. Each was counted apart by its own opening.
counted_item_by_item.A letter and what it encloses: General Washington's letter of 10 May is counted with Sir Guy Carleton's letter that it encloses; General Greene's letters of 28 and 29 August with General Leslie's letter and General Gist's report; General Greene's letter of 31 May with General Wayne's letter, which the New-Hampshire Gazette prints alone (as X-1810-01, and 1779's General Putnam letter, X-1779-03).
counted_item_by_item.Printed again counts again: The Pennsylvania Packet printed the orders of 10 January in six issues, and the King's speech of 27 November 1781, Lord Cornwallis's letter, Sir Guy Carleton and Admiral Digby's letter and Congress's resolutions of 4 October twice each.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote or recite an item: Not counted (C-07): papers that quote Sir Guy Carleton and Admiral Digby's letter inside other texts in October to December; states' proclamations that recite Congress's proclamation of thanksgiving; a state assembly's resolutions in the Connecticut Courant of 29 October that repeat the preamble of Congress's resolutions of 4 October; the New-Jersey Journal's comment that quotes the King's speech of 27 November 1781.
counted_item_by_item.Extracts without the opening: Not counted (C-06): the New-Hampshire Gazette's extract of the letter from Paris of 9 August (its second paragraph, under the same heading), and its extract of General Greene's letter of 31 May ('Flying parties of the British cavalry ...'), printed after it had printed General Wayne's letter.

for_user_decision.The first part in the autumn: As built: 22 items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted, 19 of them from September to December, when only the four year-round papers (the Pennsylvania Packet, the Connecticut Courant, the New-Jersey Gazette and the New-Hampshire Gazette) survive; with the 11 chosen stories, 30 stories in all. The rule's first part reads 'every newspaper that survives for their weeks', however few survive; the audit could ask for more papers (Y-THIN, 'Reopen if').
for_user_decision.The choice under the amended rule (B1): As built: 13 items chosen in 11 stories (General Greene's letter of 21 May is a sub-story of an admitted parent; Congress's resolutions of 12 August stand with Sir Guy Carleton and Admiral Digby's letter under a parent), so that every month from January to September has a story; the other eligible items listed as not chosen with their counts. Any not-chosen item can be added after a scan check of its printings.
for_user_decision.Digests among the items printed by every: As built (C-09): the news by the ship Apollo (4 of 4), the substance of the Leyden papers (printed in parts), the news a Salem cartel brought, and the news by the ship Carolina (4 of 4, one paper rewording its first sentence) are runs of unrelated reports and are not admitted, as 1805's news by the Palmyra and 1808's by the Camilla.
for_user_decision.A letter with its enclosure, printed in: As built: General Greene's letter of 31 May with General Wayne's letter is printed by all five papers that survive for its weeks, counting the New-Hampshire Gazette, which prints General Wayne's letter alone; without that printing it is in 4 of 5 and would be chosen, not admitted by the first part.
for_user_decision.Extracts without the opening: As built (C-06): the letter from Paris of 9 August and the Paris paragraph on Mr. Franklin and Mr. Jay with the Count de Aranda are each in 3 of the 4 surviving papers by their openings, below the bar.
for_user_decision.Both sides: As built (R-02): the Royal Gazette of Charleston's own report of Savannah's evacuation, the British commanders' letters (Lord Cornwallis, Sir Guy Carleton and Admiral Digby, General Leslie) and Governor Elliot's letter as a Cork paper printed it are admitted and described as theirs; the Amsterdam handbill as the papers describe it.
for_user_decision.Single surviving issues: As built (as X-1779-02): the New-York Gazette's 2 issues, the Royal South-Carolina Gazette's 3 and the New-Jersey Journal's 9 count among the papers that survive for an item's weeks when they fall in its window.
